Annul

uh-NUL · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To annul is to declare something legally invalid, as though it never existed.

The court agreed to annul the contract after discovering both parties had been misled.

Worked Example

A marriage can be annulled rather than divorced if certain legal conditions were never actually met.

This wasn't simply ending an agreement -- it was declaring that, legally, it had never truly existed at all, which is exactly annul.

How Annul Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

invalidate

invalidate: make something no longer legally valid

void

void: cancel the legal force of something

Antonyms

ratify

ratify: give official approval to something, making it valid

How Strong Is It? — cancel → annul → void

cancel vs. annul

cancel vs. annul: Canceling an agreement simply ends it going forward; annulling it declares that, legally, it never existed at all.

void vs. annul

void vs. annul: Annul and void both mean legally invalid; annul is most often used specifically for marriages and formal contracts.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — an-

prefix — an-: to, toward (Latin (ad-))

root — nul

root — nul: none, nothing (Latin (nullus))

Put it together

Put it together: Annul comes from Latin ad- ('to') + nullus ('none') -- literally 'to reduce to nothing.'

Use the root in a new word: null

Use the root in a new word: null: The same nullus root gives us the everyday word null, 'having no value or force,' as in "null and void."
